## Goal

Demonstrate the central limit theorem

### Subgoals

-   Learn about RMarkdown (the thing you're reading now)
-   Refactor some code, think about simplification

### Prerequisites for the central limit demonstration

-   generator of numbers from some distribution
-   give some impression of the distribution
-   display the distribution of the means

Let's have a look at how to create some skewed distributions with
built-in R functions

```{r distributions}

# The following example was taken from: https://statisticsglobe.com/draw-normal-left-right-skewed-distributions-r

set.seed(35486)                    # Create random distributions
data <- data.frame(x1 = rbeta(1000, 10, 2),
                   x2 = rbeta(1000, 5, 2),
                   x3 = rnorm(1000),
                   x4 = rbeta(1000, 2, 5),
                   x5 = rbeta(1000, 2, 10))

head(data)                         # Print head of data
```

As you can see, we're using the beta distribution, which is defined as

$\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) = \displaystyle \frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}$

where

$\mathrm{B}(\alpha, \beta)=\displaystyle \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha + \beta)}$

and $\Gamma$ is the Gamma function:
$\Gamma(z) = \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{z-1} e^{-t}\mathrm dt$

see also <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution>

All of this is not very relevant, but to show how to write maths:
<https://rpruim.github.io/s341/S19/from-class/MathinRmd.html>

## Here are some plots to show what the distributions look like graphically

Here I've used 'base R' functions, because we're going to talk about
ggplot2 later in this course.

```{r densityplots, echo=FALSE}
plot(density(data$x1), col = 2,    # Overlay all columns as densities
     xlim = c(- 3, 3),
     ylim = c(0, 5),
     main = "Comparison of Distributions",
     xlab = "Value"
     )

lines(density(data$x2), col = 3)
lines(density(data$x3), col = 4)
lines(density(data$x4), col = 5)
lines(density(data$x5), col = 6)

legend("topleft",                  # Add legend to plot
       legend = c("Beta(10, 2)",
                  "Beta(5, 2)",
                  "Normal(0, 1)",
                  "Beta(2, 5)",
                  "Beta(2, 10)"),
       col = 2:6,
       lty = 1,
       cex = 0.8)

```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to
prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

## Refactoring: adding functionality

We'd like to be able to set the number of datasets, and the number of
samples per dataset. Copy the code block from above (not very DRY, but
you will have the history of your thought process in this document)

the generate_dataset function should now take some arguments, being n
for the number of datasets, and m for the number of samples in each
dataset

We're *refactoring*, so make sure that the **generate_dataset()** call
still works.

```{r first parameters}
generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000) {

  datasets <- replicate(
    n,
    rbeta(m, shape1 = 10, shape2 = 2),
    simplify = FALSE
  )

  names(datasets) <- paste0("dataset_", seq_len(n))

  return(datasets)
}

test_refactored_1 <- generate_dataset(n = 3, m = 1000)

length(test_refactored_1)
length(test_refactored_1[[1]])
```

## Different alpha and beta arguments

Copy your refactored (working) code again and now add code to vary alpha
and beta values for the rbeta function. Again, make sure the
argument-less call gives the same results as before.

```{r add alpha and beta parameters}
generate_dataset <- function(
  n = 300,
  m = 1000,
  alpha = 10,
  beta = 2
) {

  datasets <- replicate(
    n,
    rbeta(m, shape1 = alpha, shape2 = beta),
    simplify = FALSE
  )

  names(datasets) <- paste0("dataset_", seq_len(n))

  return(datasets)
}

# Right-skewed beta distribution
right_skewed <- generate_dataset(alpha = 2, beta = 5)

# Left-skewed beta distribution
left_skewed <- generate_dataset(alpha = 5, beta = 2)

# Symmetric beta distribution
symmetric <- generate_dataset(alpha = 2, beta = 2)

# Calculate their sample means
right_means <- calculate_mean_values(right_skewed)
left_means <- calculate_mean_values(left_skewed)
symmetric_means <- calculate_mean_values(symmetric)
```

## Ambitious exercise

So far we have only used rbeta functions. Now make it possible to choose
your function in the **generate_dataset** call

Hints:

-   You can pass a function as an argument, and call this function by
    using the argument name in your function

-   Note that the random number functions all start with the number of
    samples, and are followed with specific arguments for the required
    distribution

-   examples are runif, rnorm, rbeta, look them up with `?`

-   You can pass *any* number of arguments by using '...' in the
    argument list. This can be passed on to functions inside your
    function body

```{r free form random argument}
# Default beta distribution
default_beta <- function(size, alpha = 10, beta = 2) {

  rbeta(size, shape1 = alpha, shape2 = beta)

}


# Generalised dataset generator
generate_dataset <- function(
  n = 300,
  m = 1000,
  FUN = default_beta,
  ...
) {

  datasets <- lapply(
    seq_len(n),
    function(i) FUN(m, ...)
  )

  names(datasets) <- paste0("dataset_", seq_len(n))

  return(datasets)
}

# Beta distribution
beta_data <- generate_dataset(
  FUN = rbeta,
  shape1 = 2,
  shape2 = 5
)

# Uniform distribution
uniform_data <- generate_dataset(
  FUN = runif,
  min = 0,
  max = 1
)

# Normal distribution
normal_data <- generate_dataset(
  FUN = rnorm,
  mean = 0,
  sd = 1
)

# Exponential distribution
exponential_data <- generate_dataset(
  FUN = rexp,
  rate = 1
)

beta_means <- calculate_mean_values(beta_data)

uniform_means <- calculate_mean_values(uniform_data)

normal_means <- calculate_mean_values(normal_data)

exponential_means <- calculate_mean_values(exponential_data)
length(beta_data)
length(beta_data[[1]])
length(beta_means)

```

# Demonstrating the Central Limit Theorem

According to the Central Limit Theorem (CLM), if we take samples with
random and independent observations and calculate the mean of each
sample, the probability distribution of these means will resemble a
normal distribution.

To demonstrate this, we sgenerate a list of 300 samples, each containing
1000 non-normally-distributed values. We then calculate the means of
each of the 300 samples and plot this and one of the original samples as
qqplots to assess their distribution.

The `generate_dataset` function creates a list of `n` datasets. The
function requires 4 arguments:

-   n = number of datasets
-   vectors = number of columns across all datasets
-   samples = number of rows across all datasets
-   calc_function = the function used to generate the data, default =
    `rbeta`

The dataset assigns the column names as "vector\_#" with \# being the
number of the column.

```{r the function}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

qqnorm(
  beta_data[[1]],
  main = "Original Beta(2,5)"
)
qqline(beta_data[[1]], col = "red")

qqnorm(
  beta_means,
  main = "Beta Sample Means"
)
qqline(beta_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(
  exponential_data[[1]],
  main = "Original Exponential"
)
qqline(exponential_data[[1]], col = "red")

qqnorm(
  exponential_means,
  main = "Exponential Sample Means"
)
qqline(exponential_means, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

qqnorm(beta_means, main = "Beta Sample Means")
qqline(beta_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(uniform_means, main = "Uniform Sample Means")
qqline(uniform_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(normal_means, main = "Normal Sample Means")
qqline(normal_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(exponential_means, main = "Exponential Sample Means")
qqline(exponential_means, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Now, a list of 1 dataset per method is created.

```{r running the function}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

qqnorm(beta_means, main = "Beta Sample Means")
qqline(beta_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(uniform_means, main = "Uniform Sample Means")
qqline(uniform_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(normal_means, main = "Normal Sample Means")
qqline(normal_means, col = "red")

qqnorm(exponential_means, main = "Exponential Sample Means")
qqline(exponential_means, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

To access the data frame within the list of data frames, list
comprehension is used to store the data frame as an object. Then, the
examples with `rbeta` (left) and `rnorm` (right) will be plotted next to
each other.

From these graphs we can observe that the original sample 1 was not
normally distributed, while the collective means dataset does appear to
be so. This proves the CLM.
